'''''Eugenia uniflora''''' is a [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Myrtaceae]], native to tropical South America's east coast, ranging from [[Suriname]], [[French Guiana]] to southern [[Brazil]], as well as [[Uruguay]] and parts of [[Paraguay]] and [[Argentina]].<ref name="Duke's Handbook"/><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/02/07/dining/07cherry.html|title=Berry Helped to Put Reality Show Chef on Top|work=[[The New York Times]]|author=Karp, David|date=February 7, 2007|access-date=January 28, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Morton, Julia|title=Fruits of warm climates |isbn=978-0-9610184-1-2 |year=1987|pages=386–8|chapter=Surinam cherry|chapter-url=http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/morton/surinam_cherry.html}}</ref>

It is also known as '''Brazilian cherry''',<ref name=elsevier/> '''Cayenne cherry''',<ref name="WofA">{{cite web|url=https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/eugenia_uniflora.htm|title=Weeds of Australia: ''Eugenia uniflora''|publisher=Queensland Government|access-date=January 28, 2019}}</ref> '''cerisier carré''',<ref name="Duke's Handbook">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=c8rg6rPsvUYC&pg=PA309|title=Duke's Handbook of Medicinal Plants of Latin America|author=Duke, James A.|page=309|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4200-4317-4}}</ref> '''monkimonki kersie''', '''ñangapirí,'''<ref>{{cite news|url=http://the.honoluluadvertiser.com/article/2007/Feb/28/il/FP702280358.html|title=A curious crop|work=[[The Honolulu Advertiser]]|date=February 28, 2007|access-date=January 28, 2019}}</ref> '''pitanga''',<ref name=elsevier>{{cite journal|title=Study of supercritical extraction from Brazilian cherry seeds (Eugenia uniflora L.) with bioactive compounds|author=Nascimento e Santos, Débora|author2=Lima de Souza, Larissa|author3=Nilson José Ferreira|author4=Lopes de Oliveira, Alessandra|journal=Food and Bioproducts Processing|pages=365–374|volume=94|publisher=[[Elsevier]]|year=2015|doi=10.1016/j.fbp.2014.04.005}}</ref> '''shimarucu''',<ref>{{Cite book |last=Proosdij |first=A.S.J. van |title=Arnoldo's Zakflora: Wat in het wild groeit en bloeit op Aruba, Bonaire en Curaçao |publisher=Walberg Pers |year=2012 |isbn=978-90-5730-162-9 |location=Zutphen |language=nl}}</ref> and '''Suriname cherry'''.<ref>{{cite news|author=Setzer, Kenneth|date=May 12, 2018|url=https://www.miamiherald.com/living/home-garden/article210141259.html|title=Yes, the Surinam cherry is edible, but that doesn't mean you're going to like it|work=[[Miami Herald]]|access-date=January 28, 2019}}</ref>

It is often used in gardens as a hedge or screen.

It produces small, ribbed fruits (2 to 4 centimetres or 3⁄4 to 1-1⁄2 in), starting as green, then ranging through orange, scarlet, and maroon as they ripen.

The tree was introduced to [[Bermuda]] for ornamental purposes, but is now out of control and listed as an [[invasive species]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://bermudaconservation.squarespace.com/surinam-cherry/ |title=Bermuda Conservation - Surinam Cherry |access-date=2012-05-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120205192045/http://bermudaconservation.squarespace.com/surinam-cherry/ |archive-date=2012-02-05 }}</ref>

The tree has also been introduced to [[Florida]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.eattheweeds.com/surinam-cherry-only-ripe-need-apply/|title=Surinam Cherry: Only Ripe Need Apply|date=24 September 2011|access-date=January 28, 2019}}</ref>

==Description==
''Eugenia uniflora'' is a large shrub or small tree with a conical form, growing slowly to {{convert|8|m}} high. When bruised, crushed, or cut, the leaves and branches have a spicy [[resin]]ous fragrance, which can cause respiratory discomfort in susceptible individuals. The leaves are without stipules, ovate, glossy, and held in opposite pairs.<ref name="WofA"/> New leaves are bronze, copper, or coppery-pinkish in color, maturing to deep glossy green, up to {{convert|4|cm|frac=4}} long. During winter, the leaves turn red.

Flowers have four white petals and are borne on long, slender stalks, with a conspicuous central cluster of white [[stamen]]s ending in yellow anthers. Flowers develop into ribbed fruits {{convert|2|to|4|cm|frac=4}} long, starting as green, then ranging through orange, scarlet, and maroon as they ripen. Because fruit-eating birds distribute the seeds, they can become a weed in suitable tropical and subtropical habitats, displacing native flora.<ref name="WofA"/>

==Uses==
===Culinary uses===
The edible fruit is a [[botanical berry]]. The taste ranges from sweet to sour, depending on the [[cultivar]] and level of ripeness (the darker red to black range is quite sweet, while the green to orange range is strikingly tart). Its predominant food use is as a flavoring and base for jams and jellies.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hargreaves|first1=Dorothy|last2=Hargreaves|first2=Bob|title=Tropical Trees of Hawaii|url=https://archive.org/details/tropicaltreesofh00doro_0|url-access=registration|year=1964|publisher=Hargreaves|location=Kailua, Hawaii|page=[https://archive.org/details/tropicaltreesofh00doro_0/page/61 61]|isbn=978-0-910690-02-7}}</ref> The fruit is high in [[vitamin C]] and a source of [[provitamin A]].

The leaves are also used for tea in certain parts of Uruguay.{{cn|date=October 2022}}

===Use as an insect repellent===
The leaves are spread on some house floors in Brazil so that they exude a smell that repels flies when crushed underfoot.{{cn|date=October 2022}}

===Medical uses===
''Eugenia uniflora'' has several significant pharmacological properties.<ref name="book1">{{cite book|author=Lim, TK|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=32rWbxUtjeMC&q=eugenia+uniflora&pg=PA623|series=Edible Medicinal And Non Medicinal Plants |chapter=''Eugenia Uniflora''|volume=3|title=Fruits|publisher=Springer |year=2012|pages=620–9|isbn=978-94-007-2534-8}}</ref> Its essential oil is [[antihypertensive drug|antihypertensive]],<ref name="book1"/><ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Consolini AE, Baldini OA, Amat AG|title=Pharmacological basis for the empirical use of Eugenia uniflora L. (Myrtaceae) as antihypertensive.|journal=[[Journal of Ethnopharmacology]]|volume=66|issue=1|pages=33–9|year=1999|pmid=10432205|doi=10.1016/s0378-8741(98)00194-9}}</ref> antidiabetic,<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Matsumura, T|author2=Kasai, M|author3=Hayashi, T|author4=Arisawa, M|author5=Momose, Y|author6=Arai, I|author7=Amagaya, S|author8=Komatsu, Y|year=2000|title=a-glucosidase Inhibitors From Paraguayan Natural Medicine, Nangapiry, The Leaves Of Eugenia Uniflora|journal=[[Pharmaceutical Biology]]|volume=38|issue=4|pages=302–7|doi=10.1076/1388-0209(200009)3841-AFT302|pmid=21214481|s2cid=21363070}}</ref> antitumor<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Ogunwande IA, Olawore NO, Ekundayo O, Walker TM, Schmidt JM, Setzer WN|title=Studies on the essential oils composition, antibacterial and cytotoxicity of Eugenia uniflora L.|journal=International Journal of Aromatherapy|volume=15|issue=3|pages=147–152|year=2005|doi=10.1016/j.ijat.2005.07.004}}</ref> and [[analgesic]],<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Amorim AC, Lima CK, Hovell AM, Miranda AL, Rezende CM|title=Antinociceptive and hypothermic evaluation of the leaf essential oil and isolated terpenoids from Eugenia uniflora L. (Brazilian Pitanga).|journal=[[Phytomedicine (journal)|Phytomedicine]]|volume=16|issue=10|pages=923–8|year=2009|pmid=19423309|doi=10.1016/j.phymed.2009.03.009}}</ref> and it has shown antiviral and antifungal activity.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Costa DP, Filho EG, Silva LM|title=Influence of fruit biotypes on the chemical composition and antifungal activity of the essential oils of Eugenia uniflora leaves.|journal=[[Journal of the Brazilian Chemical Society]]|volume=21|issue=5|pages=851–8|year=2010|doi=10.1590/s0103-50532010000500012|display-authors=etal|url=http://repositorio.bc.ufg.br/bitstream/ri/16301/5/Artigo%20-%20Deomar%20Pl%c3%a1cido%20da%20Costa%20-%202010.pdf|doi-access=free}}</ref> It has performed against microorganisms such as ''Trichomonas gallinae'' (in vitro),<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Ibikunle GF, Adebajo AC, Famuyiwa FG, Aladesanmi AJ, Adewunmi CO|title=In-vitro evaluation of anti-trichomonal activities of Eugenia uniflora leaf.|journal=Afr J Tradit Complement Altern Med|volume=8|issue=2|pages=170–6|year=2011|pmid=22238499|pmc=3252693}}</ref> ''Trypanosoma cruzi''<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Santos KK, Matias EF, Tintino SR, Souza CE, Braga MF, Guedes GM, Rolón M, Vega C, de Arias AR, Costa JG, Menezes IR, Coutinho HD|title=Anti-Trypanosoma cruzi and cytotoxic activities of Eugenia uniflora L.|journal=Exp. Parasitol.|volume=131|issue=1|pages=130–2|year=2012|pmid=22426246|doi=10.1016/j.exppara.2012.02.019|doi-access=free}}</ref> and ''Leishmania amazonensis''.<ref name="book1"/><ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Rodrigues KA, Amorim LV, de Oliveira JM, Dias CN, Moraes DF, Andrade EH, Maia JG, Carneiro SM, Carvalho FA|title=Eugenia uniflora L. Essential Oil as a Potential Anti-Leishmania Agent: Effects on Leishmania amazonensis and Possible Mechanisms of Action.|journal=[[Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine]]|year=2013|pmid=23533469|pmc=3590759|doi=10.1155/2013/279726|volume=2013|article-number=279726|doi-access=free}}</ref>
